summary:
Niger State stands under Nigeria's national framework, which applies here as it does elsewhere in the country. The findings below are specific to Niger State.

Niger State is one of the states that adopted Sharia criminal provisions in the wave that began with Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law, promulgated on 27 October 1999 and in force from 27 January 2000. Human Rights Watch's 2004 survey of that wave names Niger State among the states concerned. Those provisions remain in force.

The state's own instrument is the Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000. It was signed on 22 February 2000, came into operation on 4 May 2000, and was gazetted in the Niger State of Nigeria Gazette, volume 25, number 8, of 9 March 2000, at pages B29 to B36. It amends Penal Code Law Cap 94, Laws of Niger State (the 1960 Penal Code), to revise the punishments set out in it.

The amendment defines adultery to include sodomy and inserts section 68A. Under that section a Muslim convicted of a listed offence, where the offence is proved against him to the Islamic evidentiary standard, receives the harsher punishment specified under Sharia; the amendment also adds amputation to the caning paragraph of section 68. Where that standard is not met, the ordinary Penal Code punishment applies. The law is not a complete Sharia penal code: it leaves the 1960 code in place and makes certain sections carry different burdens of proof and different punishments when applied to Muslims than when applied to non-Muslims.

For a visitor, the consequence is that a Muslim traveller whose conduct falls within the listed offences and who is identified to the authorities stands under a harsher parallel legal frame in Niger State than the national law alone would impose. Travellers who are not Muslim remain under the ordinary Penal Code provisions.

No arrest, prosecution, conviction or sentencing in Niger State under the 2000 amendment appears in the sources reviewed. The state-level exposure documented here is statutory rather than evidenced by enforcement.
tangentialFactors:
The full text of Niger State's Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 is reproduced in a scholarly sourcebook on Sharia implementation in northern Nigeria, which makes the state's statutory position verifiable in detail even though no enforcement record for the state was located.

The amendment's harsher track is triggered by the defendant's religion and by the standard of proof available against him, so the same conduct carries different exposure depending on how the case is proved and on the religion recorded for the accused. Corporal punishment, including amputation, forms part of the state's sentencing frame.
localsOnly:
For residents of Niger State, the operative distinction is religious status. A Muslim resident convicted of a listed offence and proved against to the Islamic evidentiary standard faces the harsher Sharia-specified punishment, including amputation added to the caning paragraph of section 68; a resident who is not Muslim, or against whom the higher standard is not met, faces the ordinary Penal Code punishment.

The amendment has been in force since 4 May 2000 and no repeal or replacement appears in the sources reviewed.
outOfScopeNotes:
Sources catalogued under the name Niger that describe the Republic of Niger's Refoundation Charter of March 2025 and its February 2026 penal code concern a different jurisdiction and have no application in Niger State, Nigeria. They are not reflected in this assessment.

Whether Niger State's Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 reaches gender identity or gender expression as distinct from sexual conduct is not established by the available sources; the provisions reproduced concern sodomy and adultery.

No arrest, charge, conviction or sentence in Niger State under the amendment was located, and national-level assessments of Nigeria's legal framework do not disaggregate enforcement data for Niger State.
